constructs.label: Str::slug()
constructs.note: The PHP-exact subset (slug/limit/upper/lower/studly/camel/snake/kebab/title/contains/startsWith/endsWith/after/before/length/replace*/squish/ucfirst/ucwords/ascii/is/finish/start/random/isUrl) - every value is verified against the real Laravel. The transliteration is portable-ascii's own table (kernel/ascii-map.data.mjs, generated by tools/ascii-map.php; tools/ascii-map-check.mjs keeps it honest), so Str::ascii/Str::slug are byte-identical to PHP 8.3 over the whole BMP.

constructs.label: Event::dispatch() (an event object)
constructs.note: The listener is a class, so the build compiles it (the event classes + the listeners, dist/src/classes.generated.mjs). The dispatch is synchronous, like Laravel's.

constructs.label: Event::dispatch() (an event name)
constructs.reason: needs an instance of a compiled event class
constructs.note: An event name has no class: the edge cannot know which listener answers, so the dispatch would be a silent no-op - dispatch the event object instead.

constructs.label: Gate::allows()
constructs.note: The policy is compiled at build time: the abilities, the guest rules, the before() hook.

constructs.label: Gate::allows() (the class-level check)
constructs.note: Laravel shifts the class name away before the ability is called.

constructs.label: Gate::authorize()
constructs.reason: it throws an AuthorizationException
constructs.note: It throws an AuthorizationException (a 403). The edge renders the app's own resources/views/errors/403.blade.php when it exists (the same as every other status error), so the working path is Gate::allows() + abort(403).

constructs.label: Gate::any()
constructs.reason: allowed: allows, denies
constructs.note: Only allows() and denies() compile.

constructs.label: Gate::define()

constructs.label: Mail::to()->send()
constructs.note: A mailable is a class: the build compiles it (the dump takes the app's Mail classes, the class compiler emits the class and the kernel's Mailable base carries Laravel's fluent surface) and the mailer sends the payload Laravel sends - the recipients, the subject and the rendered view (the mailable's data goes into the view). The byte-for-byte proof is the shadow: the PHP oracle captures Laravel's MessageSent event (the from/to/cc/bcc/replyTo/subject/html/text) and the harness compares those fields with the kernel mailer's outbox - all 8 fields are identical, the log line is not compared. The methods the kernel mailer does not implement (raw, html, queue, later) fail loud.

constructs.label: Mail::send() (a view name)
constructs.reason: a view name is not a payload at the edge
constructs.note: Laravel's Mailer::send() has two shapes: a Mailable INSTANCE (it is sent as it is) and a VIEW NAME (Laravel renders the view with the data and sends THAT - the route answers 200 and the mail goes out). The edge has only the first shape: the compiled mailer carries a payload (a compiled Mailable, or an object with to/subject/html), so a view name throws at request time ("mail(): the message is not a payload") and the route answers 500 - the build refuses the view shape instead of shipping a route that 500s where Laravel sends the mail. A mailable still compiles (Mail::send(new OrderMail()) and Mail::to($user)->send(new OrderMail())); a dynamic first argument is NOT refused (it can hold a mailable and the build cannot prove which it is - refusing it would refuse a legal send).

constructs.label: Queue::push()
constructs.reason: the job would never run at the edge
constructs.note: The FACADE is what stays refused here: Queue::push() takes a class-name string the edge cannot resolve to a compiled class, so nothing would consume the row - Job::dispatch() on a compiled job class is the supported form (M63). Without a consumer the job would never run at the edge: the worker has no queue handler, so nothing consumes the queue binding, and the binding carries a JSON body, not a PHP job. The paths that work: a Cloudflare Queues binding with a consumer you write (a limited version is on the Workers free plan; the paid plan charges per operation), or a D1 table the cron trigger reads (a compiled job class writes the row through Job::dispatch() - M63 - or a port handler does). In Laravel the job is queued (or run inline by the sync driver) and the route answers 200.

constructs.label: Job::dispatch() on a compiled job class
constructs.note: A job class the build compiles (app/Jobs): dispatch() writes a row into the D1 lw_jobs table and the CRON TRIGGER drains it, so the job runs after the response (Laravel's database driver). The build refuses the push when the worker has no cron trigger - the job would never run - and it also refuses a push whose job class did NOT compile: the drain builds its handler map from the compiled classes, so a job the class compiler refused has no handle() for the drain and the row would be dropped unseen. Laravel's own job traits (Dispatchable, Queueable, InteractsWithQueue, SerializesModels) are allowed - their members are answered at the call site or are PHP-serializer-only - but a body that CALLS one of their members ($this->release(3)) is refused. The Queue FACADE (Queue::push) stays refused: it takes a class-name string the edge cannot resolve to a compiled class.

constructs.label: Storage::disk() (the default disk)
constructs.note: The default disk is the compiled object store (the D1 blob store, or R2 when bound).

constructs.label: Storage::disk() (a named disk)
constructs.reason: has ONE object store
constructs.note: A named disk needs a bucket of its own (R2 asks for a credit card); the compiled rung has one store.

constructs.label: Cache::tags()
constructs.reason: the compiled cache store is the D1 `database` store
constructs.note: The compiled cache store is the D1 database store, which has no tags: in Laravel this route 500s with BadMethodCallException("This cache store does not support tagging."); the build refuses the route before it ships (stricter than Laravel, not a parity), and a taggable store (redis/memcached) is not compiled.

constructs.label: Blade @extends (a layout)
constructs.note: The sections travel to the layout (the shadow harness proves the bytes).

constructs.label: Model::paginate()

constructs.label: The translation helper (__())
constructs.note: The strings are dumped at build time (the app's lang/ files + the framework's fallback); the place-holders are replaced like Laravel does.

constructs.label: A PHP cast ((string) $x)
constructs.note: The scalar casts with PHP's own semantics: (string), (int), (bool), (float).

constructs.label: The (object) cast ((object) $x)
constructs.note: PHP's cast to stdClass (rt.objectCast, oracle-probed): a list becomes an object keyed by the stringified indices, an object is answered as-is, null is the empty object, a scalar wraps under scalar. The result carries the stdClass marker, so json_encode() answers {}/{"0":..} and never the array shape ([]) - json_decode() with $assoc = false and the object model cast mark the same way

constructs.label: Null-safe access ($a?->b)
constructs.note: PHP's ?->: a null/undefined receiver answers null, and that null propagates through any later -> links in the same chain (rt.nsprop, rt.nsmethod for the method form).

constructs.label: Route-model binding (a typed param)
constructs.note: The model comes from the route segment (Laravel's implicit binding); a missing model is a 404.

constructs.label: Eloquent relations ($post->comments())
constructs.reason: is not compiled (an Eloquent relation?)
constructs.note: A relation is not compiled: the build stops (LW003). The eager loading (with()) is not compiled at the edge either - the relations are a planned milestone (M64), so a route that reads one needs a port handler until then.

constructs.label: File upload ($request->file())
constructs.note: The multipart body is parsed at the edge: the file object carries the metadata (the name, the type the browser declared, the size) and the store (the app's default disk). Byte-proven by the shadow harness.

constructs.label: The upload is stored ($file->storeAs())
constructs.note: The object store (the D1 blob store on the free plan, R2 with a bucket of its own): the path is the disk-relative one Laravel returns (trim($path.'/'.$name, '/')).

constructs.label: The upload is stored under a random name ($file->store())
constructs.note: The name is a random hash (Str::random(40)) + the extension; the extension comes from the type the browser declared (Laravel sniffs the content with finfo).

constructs.label: The content type of the upload ($file->getMimeType())
constructs.reason: it reads the file's content type (finfo)
constructs.note: The content type is read from the file's bytes (finfo): the edge cannot sniff the content like PHP does, so the build stops (LW003).

constructs.label: A mimes/mimetypes rule on an upload
constructs.note: PHP compares what finfo sniffs; the edge reads the image HEADER instead (kernel/image.mjs) and answers with the same guessExtension() map Symfony uses - so mimes:jpg,png,webp (and mimetypes:image/jpeg,...) answer Laravel's verdict, including the jpg/jpeg merge: guessExtension() answers jpg for image/jpeg and the vendor adds BOTH names, so mimes:jpeg ACCEPTS a real JPEG (ValidatesAttributes::validateMimes() :1764-1766). A parameter naming any other content (pdf, svg, docx, bmp) still fails loud (LW002): that verdict would be a guess.

constructs.label: A mimes rule naming a format the edge cannot sniff
constructs.reason: it reads the file's *content* type through finfo
constructs.note: mimes compiles only for the formats the header read can name (jpg, jpeg, png, gif, webp, avif, heic, heif): a parameter naming any other content (pdf, svg, docx, bmp) stops the build (LW002) and NAMES the parameter, because the verdict PHP reaches comes from finfo.

constructs.label: An image/dimensions rule on an upload
constructs.note: image and dimensions are getimagesize(), a HEADER read (ValidatesAttributes::validateImage/validateDimensions): the edge reads the same header (kernel/image.mjs) and applies the same named checks, so the verdict is Laravel's. A mimes/mimetypes parameter naming a format that read cannot sniff stays refused, like any other finfo rule.

constructs.label: The files bag as a method ($request->files())
constructs.reason: in Laravel it is a property (Symfony's FileBag), not a method
constructs.note: In Laravel $request->files is a property (Symfony's FileBag), not a method: the build stops (LW002) and points at $request->file() / $request->allFiles().

constructs.label: An OPTIONS route
constructs.note: The compiled side answers Laravel's automatic OPTIONS response (200 + the Allow header - byte-proven); a CORS config makes the build skip the route.

constructs.label: A relation read as a property ($post->comments)
constructs.reason: is not compiled (a relation or an accessor?)
constructs.note: A relation (or an accessor) read as a property is not compiled: the build stops (LW003). It used to answer null - a wrong answer, silently.

constructs.label: A rule object (Rule::file()->max())
constructs.reason: a rule object
constructs.note: A rule object in a CONTROLLER's validate() call is a class: the compiler cannot evaluate it at build time (the rules live in the controller's source), so the rule would be silently ignored and the validation would differ. The build stops and names what it would take. (In a FormRequest the dump normalizes the object to its string form - the row below.)

constructs.label: A rule object in a FormRequest
constructs.note: The FormRequest dump reads the rules Laravel itself builds and NORMALIZES a rule object to its string form (Laravel hands the validator the object and the validator reads that string): Rule::in(['a','b']) becomes in:"a","b" - which the kernel parses exactly like Laravel (M61a). A CONDITIONAL rule object is refused (the row below).

constructs.label: A conditional rule object in a FormRequest
constructs.note: A conditional rule object (Rule::requiredIf(true), Rule::when(...)) is refused: its string form is the CONDITION evaluated at build time (RequiredIf::__toString() returns 'required' or ''), so the edge would bake the build-time branch into the rule - a request Laravel accepts could be rejected (or the other way round). The dump stops with that reason (LW003).

constructs.label: prepareForValidation() (overridden)
constructs.note: The hook is COMPILED: the build compiles the FormRequest class (the dump registers it), the compiled handler runs the hook BEFORE the validation (Laravel's order - ValidatesWhenResolvedTrait::validateResolved), and the input the hook prepares is what the rules see. The compiled class extends the kernel's kernel/form-request.mjs - the request surface the hook uses (merge(), input(), all()).

constructs.label: A FormRequest that overrides after() / validationData() / passedValidation()
constructs.note: All three hooks run in the compiled lifecycle, in Laravel's order: validationData() is the data source, after() registers its RETURN VALUE as a validator callback, and passedValidation() runs after the rules pass. Proven by the shadow (POST /hooked-request-demo 422/422 for the after() refusal and 200/200 carrying the passedValidation marker). The hook parameter needs its TYPE HINT (Validator $validator, and the same on the callbacks the hook registers through $validator->after(...)): an untyped parameter is LW002 (the class compiler cannot infer the validator), and the route that injects the class is then STOPPED with that reason instead of shipping a handler that answers 500 (audit #891). after() returns a single callable in the proven shape.

constructs.label: A FormRequest that overrides withValidator()
constructs.note: Laravel calls the hook with the validator right after it is built (Foundation/Http/FormRequest.php:110), so the app's custom messages and its after() callbacks run. The compiled class carries the hook and the lifecycle calls it with the kernel's validator, in Laravel's order. Proven by the shadow (POST /hooked-request-demo 422/422 byte-identical when withValidator() refuses the flag) and by the compiled handler's hooks: [...] list. The hook parameter needs its TYPE HINT (Validator $validator, and the same on the callbacks the hook registers through $validator->after(...)): an untyped parameter is LW002 (the class compiler cannot infer the validator), and the route that injects the class is then STOPPED with that reason instead of shipping a handler that answers 500 (audit #891). after() returns a single callable in the proven shape.

constructs.label: A listener that injects a service
constructs.reason: the build does not compile it
constructs.note: A service the build does not compile: the edge has no container and no file for it, so the constructor dependency is a build error (the build names the class). A service the build DOES compile is injected (the edge builds it) and a framework service is adapted (the worker hands the live one down).

constructs.label: A queued listener (ShouldQueue)
constructs.reason: is queued (ShouldQueue)
constructs.note: Laravel pushes a queued listener to the queue (it runs later); the edge's queue path runs a JOB class (app/Jobs) through the cron drain, and a queued listener is not compiled as one, so running it inline would be a different behaviour. The build stops and the route that dispatches the event names the reason.

constructs.label: A listener that injects an app service the build compiles
constructs.note: The edge builds the service itself: the build compiles it (the class + the services it injects) and the runtime hands it to the listener. The dependency is recorded in the compiled class, so the edge never guesses.

constructs.label: A listener that injects a framework service (the mailer)
constructs.note: The edge has no container: the worker hands the live service down (the mailer) and the compiled listener gets it. Its async methods are awaited in the compiled body (a promise must never leak into the response).

constructs.label: A listener that pushes to the queue
constructs.reason: Queue::push() is not supported
constructs.note: The refusal holds in a compiled class too: Queue::push() names the job as a class-name string, which the edge cannot resolve to a compiled class, so nothing would consume the row (the compiled path is Job::dispatch(), M63).

constructs.label: A listener that uses a tagged cache
constructs.reason: Cache::tags() is not supported
constructs.note: The D1 database store has no tags: in Laravel this route 500s with BadMethodCallException("This cache store does not support tagging."); the build refuses the route before it ships (stricter than Laravel, not a parity).

constructs.label: A broadcast listener (ShouldBroadcast)
constructs.reason: is a broadcast listener (ShouldBroadcast)
constructs.note: Laravel broadcasts the event to the channels after the response (the broadcast itself is queued). The edge has no broadcast driver, so the notification would never be sent - a silent no-op, so the build stops and the route that dispatches the event names the reason.

constructs.label: A listener dispatched after the commit (ShouldDispatchAfterCommit)
constructs.reason: is dispatched after the commit (ShouldDispatchAfterCommit)
constructs.note: Laravel defers the listener until the database transaction is committed. The edge has no transaction, so the timing would differ - the build stops and the route that dispatches the event names the reason.

constructs.label: Event::dispatchUntil() (the halt variant)
constructs.reason: it stops the chain at the first non-null answer
constructs.note: Laravel's dispatchUntil() stops the chain at the first non-null answer and returns it. The compiled dispatch runs EVERY listener and answers the array of the responses, so the compiled rung cannot answer Laravel's value here - it fails loud with the halt semantics named.

constructs.label: an API resource (return new PostResource($post))
constructs.note: The controller answers a JsonResource; the Router's prepareResponse() wraps it in a ResourceResponse - {"data": {...}, ...with($request)} (JsonResource::toArray + the $wrap key, ResourceResponse.php:31-52). The app declares only toArray()/with(); the rest is the kernel base. Byte-proven by the shadow (GET /resource-demo identical) and by compiler/tests/resource-class.test.mjs; the audit probes it as a controller fragment with the class registry the build passes. constructs.label: A FormRequest that overrides validator()
constructs.note: Laravel asks the app's own factory for the validator (FormRequest::getValidatorInstance()), so an override decides the rules, the messages and the factory itself. constructs.label: A try/catch/finally statement
